extracted.intended_audience: scholars and researchers in humor studies, linguistics, and cognitive science
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical evaluation and refinement of a script-based, multi-level model of jokes (the General Theory of Verbal Humor). Focuses on logical/cognitive mechanisms, levels of representation, and criteria that make a text a joke and a joke successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of "logical mechanisms" (cognitive mechanisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors adopt the term "logical mechanism" to refer to mechanisms often discussed with terminology/notation from mathematical logic or metaphorical extensions; technically these mechanisms are probably "cognitive."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes mechanisms such as negation, Chiasmus, false priming, and figure-ground reversal. Caution: the term "logical" is ambiguous; the authors use it for historical/mnemonic reasons but acknowledge "cognitive" might be more accurate. The mechanisms are the building blocks by which scripts are manipulated in jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure-ground reversal (three senses; authors' restricted sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forabosco notes several senses of figure/ground reversal; the authors adopt a restricted, third sense — the "relational Inversion" — intended as a REAL VS. UNREAL role swapping for some elements in the joke situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use the figure/ground label too broadly. The term is a convenient mnemonic for role-swapping phenomena in jokes (related to Gestalt perceptive phenomena like Rubin's cup). Other logical mechanisms (negation, chiasmus, false priming) help disambiguate usage and reduce confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification / Acceptance (two aspects of a humorous fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Aubouin: the two basic aspects of a humorous fact are "incongruity" and "acceptance/justification." Acceptance describes hearer behavior; justification denotes the condition in which the object can elicit this acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance is often brief and superficial — a momentary masking of absurdity. It need not be a factual error by the hearer; acceptance can be a "willing suspension of disbelief" or imposition of a paralogic/pseudologic on the situation. A successful humorous text must provide conditions (justification) that allow the hearer to accept two incongruous elements simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors enabling humor: errors of judgment and of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Aubouin divides errors into (1) errors of judgment (similarities, bad observation conditions, lack of experience, prejudice, fatigue, hasty generalizations, etc.) and (2) errors connected with language (similarity of sounds including homonyms and paronyms, ambiguities — semantic and syntactic, literal interpretation of frozen metaphors, puns, alliterations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These errors can be treated as constituents of a special faulty logic (paralogic) legitimate for humor. The presence of such errors or rule relaxations in the text can provide the justification/conditions for acceptance, but actual factual deception of the hearer is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metalinguistic suspension (puns and rule-suspension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns have a metalinguistic aspect: rules of the object-language are suspendable in the metalanguage, allowing superficially incompatible meanings to be reconciled without actual error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metalinguistic devices to permit temporary reconciliation of disparate meanings (example: Chomsky's 'COLORLESS GREEN IDEAS SLEEP FURIOUSLY' accepted as grammatical in a metalinguistic frame). This explains why puns do not require the hearer to be truly misled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy and ordering of representational levels (precede-follow relation among KRs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors propose a hierarchy of levels of representation (KRs) with a precede-follow relation: one level influences/restricts (but does not constrict) choices at lower levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a simpler linear/vector model (<a,b,c,...>) for ordering before moving to complex partial orders. A hierarchical ordering is justified when relations among entities are of interest and when higher levels can be shown to restrict lower-level choices; unordered sets lose this explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive/explanatory/resolution function of a humor theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory should provide a resolution mechanism (reverse-analysis generative procedure) that separates a (potential) joke from a nonjoke, giving predictive power about what entities belong to the privileged set of jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory need not claim psychological realism about mental instantiation of levels, but should specify rule-governed operations that can (in principle) predict and explain which texts are jokes. Lack of an explicit algorithm does not invalidate a theory if it supplies a coherent resolution function.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Real-life" versus "artificially concocted" jokes (acceptability test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'real-life' joke is created and then passes an acceptability test by being memorized and repeated by people; this social transmission marks acceptability. The distinction relates to degree/quality of script Opposition but also to empirical occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing jokes, consider whether the example is merely illustrative (artificial) or has social currency (real-life). Real-life status correlates with acceptability and, often, perceived quality, though bad jokes can become widespread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script Opposition as primary quality criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality or degree of Opposition between scripts is a central criterion for judging a joke ('good' vs 'bad' joke).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate which scripts are opposed and how strongly; primitive or squalid oppositions tend to produce low-quality jokes. Script opposition alone is not the sole determinant — all components must fit together above some threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotype activation and selection (single-activation principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally only one of several available stereotypes about a target is activated in a joke; if two stereotypes clash or it's unclear which is evoked, the joke will suffer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing sophisticated jokes requires careful selection of the appropriate stereotype. While more selection/work can improve sophistication, beyond a threshold the cognitive effort undermines the joke and may 'kill' it for many or all hearers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistication threshold / acceptable cognitive work
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a threshold of 'work' or sophistication: some work is needed for sophisticated jokes, but too much complexity or required inference will reduce or eliminate humor for many hearers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating jokes, balance sophistication against accessibility. Empirical study of 'sophistication and its expression in language' is recommended to determine appropriate thresholds.
